newsitem.title: USA: Alliance builders outpace other hi-techs - study.
newsitem.headline: Alliance builders outpace other hi-techs - study.

text.p: The most successful high tech companies are the efficient alliance builders not those which charge ahead at breakneck speed , according to a study released Tuesday.

Andersen Consulting said its two-year study of the world's top electronic systems companies determined the tortoise who slowly builds allies can outdo a visionary hare in the race for electronics industry leadership.

"Our study finds that the best performers in this industry are those who demonstrate they can exploit uncertainty rather than fall victim to it," said Carleton Kilmer, worldwide managing partner of Andersen's Electronics and High Tech practice.

Researchers who conducted the study said its results contradict the theory of Harvard Business School Prof. Michael Porter, a leading strategy guru, that companies can excel by developing one essential core competency.
"Porter's model doesn't appear to apply to this industry," said Kilmer, who heads an operating unit with more than $350 million in annual turnover and 4,000 staff.

At a press conference at Andersen's Center for Strategic Technology in Palo Alto, the consulting firm said the best performing high tech companies steer away from traditional strategic planning and rely instead on multiple and shifting sources of competitive advantage.

"The high performers value collaboration over competition," said Kilmer. In fact, high performers were found to have more than 2.5 times as many collaborative and investment initiatives as medium and low performers.
But they also take more time in deciding on forming alliances than lower performers - averaging 4.5 months compared with three for those with poorer records.

Furthermore, the most successful high tech companies take longer to enter a new product market and to adopt new technologies, but with better results in delivering their products on time and in satisfying their targeted markets.

As a sign of the impact of rapid change in the market, Andersen said fully 42 percent of companies who were in the world's top 150 electronic systems providers in 1995 had dropped off the list 10 years later, and nearly a third slipped in rank while less than a quarter rose.

A high percentage of respondents in North America - 86 percent - said they perceive themselves to have actually changed the rules of the game in their industry, compared to 71 percent in Asia and just 27 percent in Europe.

Developments in products and marketing each account for about a third of the means by which companies say they are changing the competitive milieu, followed by strategy and operational advantages, companies said.

Kilmer argued that semiconductor makers -- such as chip giant Intel Corp. and neighboring Advanced Micro Devices will take an increasing share of high tech margins. Anderson forecasts this will rise to 23.4 percent in the year 2001 from a peak of 19.1 percent in 1995.

Kathleen Eisenhardt, a Stanford University professor who helped direct the project, likened the skills a company needs to prosper in technology to a versatile baseball pitcher with a variety of pitching styles.

Russel Craig, an Andersen partner who directed the Global Economics Study, said successful companies in the future will be those who change and refresh their business partnerships frequently and use these alliances as a preemptive weapon against their rivals. (sam.perry@reuters.com, Palo Alto, +1 415 846 5400)
